text: Karl Ernst Adolf Anderssen (6 July 1818 – 13 March 1879) was a German chess master who won the 1851 and 1862 international tournaments but lost matches to Paul Morphy in 1858 and to Wilhelm Steinitz in 1866. He is generally regarded as the world's leading chess player from 1851 to 1858 and the leading active player from 1862 to 1866, although the title of World Chess Champion did not exist at the time. Anderssen became the most successful tournament player in Europe, winning over half the events he entered, including the strong Baden-Baden 1870 tournament, and achieved most of his successes after turning 50. He is famous for his brilliant sacrificial attacking play, especially in the Immortal Game (1851) and the Evergreen Game (1852). He played a key role in advancing chess problem composition, transitioning from the "Old School" to modern, elegant, and complex compositions. He was known as one of the most likeable masters and became an elder statesman of the game, sought for advice or arbitration. Born in Breslau (now Wrocław, Poland) in the Prussian Province of Silesia in 1818, he lived there most of his life, sharing a home with his widowed mother and unmarried sister, and never married. He graduated from the public gymnasium in Breslau in 1847 at age 29 and studied mathematics and philosophy at university, later becoming an instructor and professor of Mathematics at the Friedrichs-Gymnasium. His career was centered on teaching mathematics, while chess remained his passion. At age nine, his father taught him chess, and as a boy, he learned strategy from a copy of William Lewis' book Fifty Games Between Labourdonnais and McDonnell (1835). In 1842, he published Aufgabe für Schachspieler, a collection of 60 chess problems, which brought him to the attention of the "Berlin Pleiades" group, and he continued publishing problems in magazines and a second collection in 1852. He became editor of Schachzeitung der Berliner Schachgesellschaft (later Deutsche Schachzeitung) in 1846 after its founder Ludwig Bledow died, holding the position until 1865. In 1848, he drew a match with Daniel Harrwitz, and due to his reputation, was invited to represent German chess at the 1851 London International Tournament. Though reluctant due to travel costs, he accepted after Howard Staunton offered to cover expenses if he failed to win a prize. His preparation in early 1851, involving over 100 games against strong opponents like Carl Mayet, Ernst Falkbeer, Max Lange, and Jean Dufresne, led to a strong performance. In the knock-out 1851 tournament, he won by defeating Lionel Kieseritzky, József Szén, Staunton, and Marmaduke Wyvill by margins of at least two games each, earning two-thirds of the £500 prize fund (about £335, equivalent to £240,000/$370,200 in 2006 money). When Anderssen and Szén agreed that if either won the tournament, the other would receive one-third of the prize, it was not considered unethical. Although Wilhelm Steinitz is now seen as the first true world champion, one of the 1851 tournament organizers referred to the contest as for "the baton of the World's Chess Champion," and Anderssen was recognized as the world's leading player despite not being called "world champion." A subsequent tournament organized by the London Chess Club a month later, which included former participants, also saw Anderssen win. Tournament opportunities remained rare, and Anderssen avoided long travels due to expense. In the 1857 Manchester tournament, a one-game-per-round knock-out event, he was eliminated in the second round. In late 1858, he lost 8–3 to Paul Morphy in a match in Paris (two wins, two draws, seven losses), with Morphy better understanding when to attack and how to prepare it, having recently defeated Johann Löwenthal, the Rev. John Owen, and Daniel Harrwitz. Morphy retired in 1859, restoring Anderssen as the strongest active player. In three games against Morphy, Anderssen played the opening 1.a3, breaking even (one loss, one draw, one win), an opening now known as Anderssen's Opening, which has never been popular in serious competition. Shortly after the 1851 tournament, he played and won two famous games: the "Immortal Game" against Lionel Kieseritzky in London on 21 June 1851, sacrificing a bishop, both rooks, and finally his queen; and the "Evergreen Game" in Berlin in 1852 against Jean Dufresne, sacrificing more than a queen and a minor piece. After the Morphy match, he played two matches against Ignác Kolisch, drawing in 1860 and narrowly winning in 1861 (5/9; won four, drew two, lost three; Kolisch was ahead at halfway). In 1862, he won the London tournament, the first international round-robin, with twelve wins out of thirteen games, losing only to the Rev. John Owen, finishing two points ahead of Louis Paulsen, who had the best early 1860s record. He then drew a match against Paulsen (3 wins, 3 losses, 2 draws) and drew another against Berthold Suhle in 1864 (3 wins, 3 losses, 2 draws). In 1866, he lost a close match to Wilhelm Steinitz (six wins, eight losses, no draws; Steinitz won the last two games), marking the point when Steinitz succeeded him as the leading active player. Although Steinitz later developed the positional approach, the 1866 match was played in the attack-at-all-costs style of the 1850s and 1860s. Ideas of a world championship had existed since the 1840s, but the 1866 match was not officially defined as such, and many opposed the title while Morphy was still alive. Anderssen remained dominant in top tournaments and personal matches against Zukertort until 1871. As tournaments became more frequent and round-robin formats were adopted, Anderssen rededicated himself to chess, studying endgames and positional play, resulting in his finest career performances in his early fifties. He achieved five first places, two second places, two third places, and a sixth place in his final year, when his health was failing. One of his first places was ahead of Steinitz, Gustav Neumann, Joseph Henry Blackburne, Louis Paulsen, and other strong players at Baden-Baden 1870, which is regarded as one of the top 20 tournaments ever. One of his third places was at the strong Vienna 1873 tournament when he was 55. About half of his tournament successes came in regional German Chess Federation championships, which were open to all nationalities and included top ten or top five players. He usually beat Zukertort in matches, but his dominance ended in 1871. The Leipzig 1877 tournament, named the "Anderssen-Feier," was held in his honor, and he finished second behind Louis Paulsen. At Leipzig, he lost a match to Paulsen (three wins, one draw, five losses); his only match win in this period was in 1868 against Johann Zukertort (eight wins, one draw, three losses). Anderssen was highly successful in European tournaments from 1851 to early 1878, taking first prize in over half of the events, with only two recorded failures: the 1857 knock-out tournament and sixth place at Paris 1878 when his health was failing. His match record was weak: out of 12 matches, he won two, drew four, and lost six. Despite being outclassed by Morphy and to a lesser extent by Steinitz, Anderssen is considered the first modern chess master. Arpad Elo retroactively calculated that Anderssen was the first player with a rating over 2600, and Chessmetrics ranks him among the top two players from 1859 to 1873 and as the strongest player in the world for seven months between 1860 and 1870. Steinitz called Anderssen one of the two greatest attacking players of his time, saying, "We all may learn from Morphy and Anderssen how to conduct a king's-side attack," and noted his honesty and honour. Although associated with the "heroic" attacking school, Anderssen opposed mindless aggression, stating, "Move that one of your pieces, which is in the worst plight, unless you can satisfy yourself that you can derive immediate advantage by an attack," a principle known as "Makogonov's rule." According to Reuben Fine, his over-the-board brilliance contrasted with an uninspired safety-first attitude in daily life. Breslau University awarded him an honorary doctorate in 1865. His attacking style, seen in games like the Immortal and Evergreen Games, is among the most famous in chess history. The "heroic" attacking school was eventually eclipsed by Steinitz's positional approach, which by 1894 was recognized as the only way to beat Steinitz. Anderssen had a lasting influence on chess problem composition, beginning in the "Old School" era, which featured realistic positions, spectacular key moves, multiple sacrifices, and few variations. He was one of the most skillful composers of his time, and his work represents the "Transition Period" between the mid-1840s and early 1860s, when game-like positions were abandoned and composing competitions (first in 1854) led to new standards. Outside chess problems, he was not a prolific author, but he edited Schachzeitung from 1846 to 1865 and co-edited Neue Berliner Schachzeitung from 1864 to 1867. Anderssen died on 13 March 1879 in his hometown, with the Deutsche Schachzeitung publishing a nineteen-page obituary; his cause of death was a heart attack. Bombing raids during World War II damaged his grave in Breslau, which after the war became part of Poland and is now known as Wrocław. In 1957, the Polish Chess Federation re-buried him in a new grave at the Osobowice Cemetery.
